title: You've been putting it off
hook: Marcus: remember how long you've delayed, and that your time has a limit (Meditations 2.4)
tomorrow: as if it were the last

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khidr: the goldsmith's fate read as allegory, and an honest flinch. Your line was hard to read.

Everybody has a list. The call to the old friend. The doctor's appointment. The drawer, the will, the apology, the book you swore you'd start. It's been there so long it's practically furniture; you don't even see it anymore. And each time you pass it, a small voice says, soon. Long ago, a Roman emperor had the same list and the same voice, and in his notebook he turned around and argued with it. Today, you've been putting it off.
screen: `THE LIST THAT'S BECOME FURNITURE.` → `A SMALL VOICE SAYS SOON.` → `YOU'VE BEEN PUTTING IT OFF.`

segments.voice: Book two, section four, begins in George Long's translation: "Remember how long thou hast been putting off these things, and how often thou hast received an opportunity from the gods, and yet dost not use it." Notice who he's talking to. Not his generals, not his son. Himself. The emperor, with an army at his command, is scolding himself for procrastinating. What things? He doesn't list them, and it isn't paperwork. The passage points inward, to the work of living by reason, calm and just, which he kept meaning to get serious about. Then it turns: understand what kind of universe you're part of, and remember that a limit of time is fixed for you. If you don't use it to clear the clouds from your mind, it will go, and you will go, and it will not come back. That's the Stoic move. They didn't think about death to be gloomy; they thought about it to wake up. The limit isn't a threat; it's a clock you can finally hear. Other traditions have their own versions. The Psalms ask God to teach us to number our days. The Buddha's last words, in the old accounts, urge his followers to strive on with diligence. Marcus puts it bluntly: you've had chance after chance, and the chances are not endless. And here's the gentle part. He doesn't call himself a failure for putting it off. He just says, remember. The list is still there, today still counts, and there is a limit, and you're inside it now.
screen: `HOW LONG HAVE YOU PUT IT OFF?` · `AN EMPEROR SCOLDS HIMSELF.` · `A LIMIT OF TIME IS FIXED.` · `NOT GLOOM: A CLOCK YOU CAN HEAR.` · then, large: `THERE IS A LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Let your list come to mind and choose one item that's waited far too long, something small enough to begin today. Picture the first step actually happening: the text typed, the number dialed, the drawer open. Then decide exactly when you'll do it, and say the time inside.
Marcus, scolding himself in his notebook for putting things off, and for how many chances he's already had. Today's word.
Your line: there is a limit. Marcus said it to himself first, and gently. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 174 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AS IF IT WERE THE LAST.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often return to 2.4 as a morning reminder, and some in modern Stoic practice keep a short daily reflection on the limits of time, sometimes called memento mori.

chat.says: Why did Marcus Aurelius think about his own death so much? Isn't that gloomy?
options: Not gloomy: remembering the limit was a way to wake up and use today.
He feared death and wrote to talk himself out of thinking about it.
Yes. He was gloomy about it and wrote to warn others away from hope.
chat.meaning: A limit of time is fixed, Marcus reminded himself. Stoics thought about death not to be gloomy, but to wake up: a clock you can finally hear.
